headline: Oil prices hit 6-month high amid fears of US strikes on Iran
summary: Brent crude surged to $116.72 per barrel as investors fear escalating tensions between the US and Iran, marking the highest price since April.
details: International crude oil prices reached a six-month high on Friday, with Brent crude rising 3.1% to $116.72 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) also climbed 3.8% to $103.27 per barrel.

The price surge is driven by investor fears that the United States may launch new attacks on Iran in the coming weeks. This follows vague comments from President Donald Trump, who stated that 'something will happen soon' regarding Iran.
The New York Times, citing US officials, reported that the US and Israel are planning new strikes on Iran following the mid-term elections.
In response, Iran's military chief announced that the country's forces are fully prepared for an 'asymmetric war' after increasing their military capabilities.

Tensions are further escalated by Houthi rebels, backed by Iran, Iran-supported Houthi rebels have continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, including drone strikes on the Shaiybah oil field and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Due to these ongoing attacks, the US State Department has ordered non-essential US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Aramco, the state-owned oil company, has instructed its employees at the main office in Dhahran to work from home or move to safe locations.
Brent crude prices have risen by 6.2% over the past week, and oil prices have been climbing for three consecutive weeks.
caption:
Oil prices have surged to their highest level in six months. Why is the global market reacting so sharply?

International crude oil prices reached a six-month high on Friday, with Brent crude rising 3.1% to $116.72 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) also climbed 3.8% to $103.27 per barrel.

The price surge is driven by investor fears that the United States may launch new attacks on Iran in the coming weeks. This follows vague comments from President Donald Trump, who stated that 'something will happen soon' regarding Iran.

The New York Times, citing US officials, reported that the US and Israel are planning new strikes on Iran following the mid-term elections.

In response, Iran's military chief announced that the country's forces are fully prepared for an 'asymmetric war' after increasing their military capabilities.

Tensions are further escalated by Houthi rebels, backed by Iran, Iran-supported Houthi rebels have continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, including drone strikes on the Shaiybah oil field and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

Due to these ongoing attacks, the US State Department has ordered non-essential US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Aramco, the state-owned oil company, has instructed its employees at the main office in Dhahran to work from home or move to safe locations.

Brent crude prices have risen by 6.2% over the past week, and oil prices have been climbing for three consecutive weeks.

topic: bangladeshis charged in canadian visa fraud
headline_marked: 209 Bangladeshis involved in [[visa fraud scheme in Canada]]
headline: 209 Bangladeshis involved in visa fraud scheme in Canada
summary: Five Bangladeshis have been charged in connection with an elaborate immigration fraud involving 243 temporary resident visa applications.
details: Five Bangladeshis have been charged in Canada over an alleged immigration fraud scheme involving 243 temporary resident visa applications for 209 Bangladeshi nationals.
According to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), investigators found fake documents and false statements in the applications to help applicants obtain visas.
Four of the accused—Rashel Mirza, Mohammed Aminul Islam, Md Mudassar Alam Bhuiyan, and Kazi Nafeez Alam—appeared at the Valleyfield courthouse in Quebec.
The fifth accused, Md Rakibul Hassan, is reportedly in Bangladesh, and an arrest warrant has been issued against him.
The investigation began after a compliance operation at a private residence in Mercier, Quebec, on July 3, 2024, leading to a formal investigation in August.
Investigators executed search warrants in Quebec and Ontario, gathering evidence that pointed to the involvement of the five accused.
The accused face three charges, including conspiring to organize the entry of people into Canada and aiding people to misrepresent material facts in immigration applications.
Immigration specialists warn that submitting forged documents can result in a visa refusal and a ban on entering Canada for at least five years.
The CBSA has advised applicants to verify all information and avoid placing blind trust in consultants who guarantee a visa.
caption:
209 Bangladeshis linked to a massive visa fraud scheme in Canada. 5 people now face charges.

Five Bangladeshis have been charged in Canada over an alleged immigration fraud scheme involving 243 temporary resident visa applications for 209 Bangladeshi nationals.

According to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), investigators found fake documents and false statements in the applications to help applicants obtain visas.

Four of the accused—Rashel Mirza, Mohammed Aminul Islam, Md Mudassar Alam Bhuiyan, and Kazi Nafeez Alam—appeared at the Valleyfield courthouse in Quebec.

The fifth accused, Md Rakibul Hassan, is reportedly in Bangladesh, and an arrest warrant has been issued against him.

The investigation began after a compliance operation at a private residence in Mercier, Quebec, on July 3, 2024, leading to a formal investigation in August.

Investigators executed search warrants in Quebec and Ontario, gathering evidence that pointed to the involvement of the five accused.

The accused face three charges, including conspiring to organize the entry of people into Canada and aiding people to misrepresent material facts in immigration applications.

Immigration specialists warn that submitting forged documents can result in a visa refusal and a ban on entering Canada for at least five years.

The CBSA has advised applicants to verify all information and avoid placing blind trust in consultants who guarantee a visa.
